title: The Effect of Crowding on Human Task Performance
research_question: What effect does density have on performance on simple and complex tasks? What role do temporal factors play?

participants.description: Experiment I: 84 boys and 42 girls (total 126) from high schools in Palo Alto, California. Experiment II: 306 high school students (18 male groups, 16 female groups). Experiment III: 180 women (ages 25-60) recruited through a temporary employment agency.
participants.recruitment: Experiment I & II: Ad in local newspaper offering $1.75/hour. Experiment III: Temporary employment agency.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Rooms of varying sizes: 160 sq ft (large), 80 sq ft (medium), and 35 sq ft (small). Subjects were placed in groups of 5 or 9. Density was manipulated by varying room size and group size, ensuring physical comfort (air conditioning, sound insulation, water cooler, desk-arm chairs, no physical contact).

measures.instrument: Proposed solutions, indicating three best ideas
Number of specific random numbers crossed out in 10 minutes
Number of different English words formed from six given letters in 8 minutes
Number of unique uses suggested for a common object (e.g., 10-gallon metal barrel) in 10 minutes (measure of divergent/creative thinking)
Number of 12 common words recalled after reading at 1 word/second
Number of clicks counted (non-fixed rhythm, 15-57 clicks)
Group-generated unique uses for a common object
Number of anagrams solved from sets of five letters in 50 minutes

findings.quote: The results can be summarized by saying that there were no effects of any kind attributable to the level of density in the rooms.

findings.consequent: Performance on forming words task (Experiment I)
findings.quote: The rooms did not differ appreciably on any task or group of tasks.

findings.consequent: Performance on individual object uses task (Experiment I)
findings.quote: high density neither facilitated nor interfered with their performance on either simple or complex tasks
there was no indication that density produced greater effects over time.
The small rooms do better almost exactly as often as they do worse; they do better on simple tasks as often as they do worse

findings.consequent: Performance on group object uses task (Experiment I)
findings.quote: on complex tasks as often as they do worse.
Clearly there are no significant effects or trends in these data.

findings.consequent: Performance on forming words task (Experiment II)

findings.quote: On the first day, groups in the smaller room did somewhat worse on the first half of the anagram task than did groups in the larger room.
once again there were no effects of any kind of density on performance.

findings.consequent: Performance on forming words task (Experiment III)
findings.quote: The large room did as well as the small room at all points, both in amount of work and number of errors.
This finding seems reliable, at least for the conditions we have employed.

findings.consequent: Performance on concentration and memory tasks
findings.quote: girls performing better on concentration and memory tasks
and less well on the more "creative" tasks.

findings.antecedent: Task repetition (second time vs. first time)
findings.quote: consistent tendency for all groups to perform better the second time they took a test than the first
the high motivation condition did more work on the crossing-out task

findings.consequent: Performance on forming-words and anagram tasks (Experiment II)

findings.quote: and was slightly inferior on the more creative forming-words and anagram tasks.

mechanisms: The paper initially hypothesized that high density acts as an aversive stimulus, raising drive level and affecting performance on simple (facilitation) and complex (interference) tasks, similar to social facilitation effects. However, the null findings led them to conclude that density per se does not function as an ordinary aversive, arousing stimulus in their experimental conditions.

The authors suggest that any effects of high density might be more complicated, primarily affecting social behaviors and interactions among people, rather than individual task performance, and would be determined by specific conditions, individual reactions, and initial relations among individuals.
moderators: Temporal factors (early vs. late performance, first vs. second day)
implementation_implications: The research suggests that high density per se, when physical discomfort and other negative consequences are controlled, does not inherently produce a decrement in individual task performance. Therefore, if logistical problems of high density can be solved, it may not be inherently 'evil' and could even be encouraged or allowed rather than discouraged, given a particular population.

limitations: The duration of crowding was limited to 4 hours, and subjects knew it was limited, which might prevent effects from appearing that would emerge with longer, indefinite exposure.

The experimental situation was relatively formal and structured, with subjects having their own chairs, specific tasks, limited verbal interaction, and no physical movement, which might not generalize to other crowded situations.
The study did not demonstrate that density *never* has an effect on performance, only that it had no effect under the particular controlled conditions employed.
The authors acknowledge that the measures of education and income used in Schmitt's (1966) study were questionable, potentially leading to inaccurate partial correlations.
Winsborough's (1965) study might have 'controlled too well' by partialling out many correlated factors, leading to implausible negative correlations between density and morbidity/disease.

paper_metadata.title: The Effect of Crowding on Human Task Performance1
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Effect of Crowding on Human Task Performance<sup>1</sup>
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In a series of three experiments, groups of people performed tasks under varying conditions of density. The tasks ranged from very simple to complex, from rote memory to a test of creativity. Subjects worked on the tasks for 4 hours at a time for two or three successive days. There were no significant effects of density on performance, nor any consistent trends.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Increased population density universally leads to negative effects on human task performance and mood.
